abstract: This paper examines the interconnected relationships among national innovation capability, firm innovation, and firm export performance in emerging countries. Utilizing datasets over the 2011–2018 period on Vietnam, a representative emerging economy with significant improvements in economic growth over the last couple of decades, the study contributes to the literature as the pioneering research linking national innovation capability to firm export performance by highlighting the role of firm innovation as an intermediary factor. We find that innovation capability at both macro and micro level significantly enhances firm export performance, with innovation providing firms with a competitive edge in international markets. Interestingly, while national innovation capability generally promotes firm innovation, it may initially crowd out private innovation until a threshold is reached, after which it complements and further drives firm innovation. Robustness checks, including those using alternative variable definitions and addressing the endogeneity problem using a two-stage least squares regression approach, confirm the reliability of the results. These findings provide valuable insights for policymakers and business practitioners on developing policies aiming at promoting firm innovation and enhancing export performance through supportive national innovation systems.
title: Unravelling the triad of national innovation capability, firm innovation and firm export performance: the case of an emerging country
title_zh: 解析国家创新能力、企业创新与企业出口绩效的三元关系：一个新兴国家的案例

abstract: This study is the first to estimate the effect of parenthood on total job absences, including both short- and long-term spells. Unlike prior work on formal sick leave records, I incorporate day-to-day absences, which account for most absence events and reflect broader margins of health and time strain. I find that mothers’ absences increase by 1.25 days per month 2 years after birth, stabilizing at 0.85 days – a 4.6–5.7% loss in annual workdays. The penalty is driven mainly by mothers’ own sickness and concentrated in long spells. It is largely unaffected by working hour or within-couple bargaining power. These findings uncover an overlooked mechanism behind the child penalty and deepen our understanding of gender inequality in labour supply.
title: Counting the days: parenthood and the gender gap in absenteeism
title_zh: 计算天数：育儿与缺勤中的性别差距
